steps.vi: Tiếng Việt hoạt động thế nào
steps.why: Before any words: what the marks mean and why tone matters.
steps.teach: Ask your teacher to say the six tones on “ma”, one at a time, and copy each one. Find out which two you mix up.
steps.tg: Model the six tones on “ma” and “ba”, slowly then at normal speed. Note which tones the learner cannot hear apart and which they cannot produce. Do not move on to words yet; five relaxed minutes on tones is enough.

steps.en: Train your ear on the tones
steps.why: You cannot say a tone you cannot hear. Ear first.
steps.teach: Say all eight words from steps 1 and 2 to your teacher. Ask them to correct only the tone, nothing else.
steps.tg: Listen to the eight words: chào, cảm ơn, dạ, không, xin lỗi, không sao, được, không được. Correct tone only. Praise anything that is close; confidence matters more than accuracy this week.

steps.vi: Nguyên âm: a ă â · o ô ơ
steps.en: Vowels: a ă â and o ô ơ
steps.why: Six vowels English does not separate. Get the mouth shape right now and everything later is easier.
steps.teach: Watch your teacher’s mouth on ơ and â, then say them while they watch yours. Write what they tell you in “My notes from class” in the mouth guide.
steps.tg: Show the mouth for a / ă / â and o / ô / ơ. The usual problems: ơ said as English “er” with rounded lips, and â not short enough. Let the learner watch your lips, then watch theirs.

steps.vi: Nguyên âm: e ê i · u ư
steps.en: Vowels: e ê i and u ư
steps.why: ư is the sound most foreigners never fix. Fix it this week.
steps.teach: Spend five minutes on ư alone. Say “thư”, “từ”, “sữa” until your teacher nods.
steps.tg: Drill ư against u: tư / tu, thư / thu, nữ / nụ. The learner should keep the tongue back and spread the lips. Check e against ê as well: xe / xê.

steps.why: Vietnamese has no single word for “you”. You pick a family word by age. This is the politeness system in one step.

items: you (a man a bit older than you); older brother
you (a woman a bit older than you); older sister
you (a friend your own age); friend
Hello (to a man a bit older).
Hello (to a woman a bit older).

steps.teach: Ask your teacher what they call you and what you should call them. Then go through five people you know and decide the right word for each.
steps.tg: Explain how you and the learner should address each other, and why. Give five real people (a waiter of 20, a landlady of 55, a taxi driver of 40…) and have the learner choose the word. Mention that tôi is always safe for a beginner.

steps.why: Prices, addresses, phone numbers, time. Numbers are the first thing you will be asked on the street.
steps.teach: Ask your teacher to say ten numbers in random order while you write them down as digits. Then swap: you say, they write.
steps.tg: Number dictation, both ways, 1 to 10 in random order. Watch bốn / bảy / tám, which beginners confuse, and the tone on một and mười.

steps.why: Now words become a conversation: hello, how are you, what is your name, where are you from.

items: Tôi khỏe, cảm ơn. Còn anh?
I am well, thanks. And you?

stops.en: Put in your own name and country

steps.teach: Have this exact conversation with your teacher three times: once reading, once looking up, once with nothing in front of you.
steps.tg: Role-play the greeting three times, the last time with no text. Swap roles so the learner also asks the questions. Replace “Ben” and “người Mỹ” with their real name and country.

steps.en: The three vowel pairs: iê, ươ, uô
steps.why: Mưa is rain, mua is buy. These three slides are where meaning changes.
steps.teach: Read these pairs to your teacher: mưa / mua, mướn / muốn, cửa / của. They tell you which one they heard.
steps.tg: Minimal pairs, learner speaks and you say which you heard: mưa / mua, mướn / muốn, cửa / của, bia / bưa. Explain the spelling rule: ia, ưa, ua at the end of a word; iê, ươ, uô when a letter follows.

steps.why: The first thing you will really use. One pattern, “Cho tôi …”, and ten things to put in it.

items: Cho tôi một ly cà phê sữa đá.

steps.teach: Your teacher is the waiter. Order a drink and a dish, ask the price, ask for the bill.
steps.tg: Play the waiter. Let the learner order with “Cho tôi một …”, ask “Bao nhiêu tiền?”, and call for the bill. Answer with real prices so they start hearing numbers in use.

steps.why: Put it together in a mock run before you do it for real.

stops.en: Learn the lines, then the mock run

steps.teach: Do the restaurant mock run with your teacher instead of the app. Then go and order something for real this week.
steps.tg: Run the restaurant scene live, with small surprises (“we are out of that”, “spicy or not?”). Set the homework: order one thing in Vietnamese before the next class and report back.

steps.why: Ngàn, trăm, triệu. Hearing a price said fast is its own skill.

items: Can you come down a little?
Can I pay by bank transfer?

steps.teach: Price dictation: your teacher says ten prices the way a seller would, you write the digits.
steps.tg: Say ten real prices at street speed (“ba chục”, “trăm rưỡi”, “hai trăm hai”) and have the learner write the number. Teach the short forms sellers use: chục, rưỡi, dropping “ngàn”.

steps.why: Left, right, straight, stop here. Enough to direct any driver.

items: Đi xe máy mất bao lâu?
How long does it take by motorbike?

steps.teach: Draw a simple map. Direct your teacher’s finger from one corner to another using only Vietnamese.
steps.tg: Map game: the learner directs you across a hand-drawn map. Add the Saigon word “quẹo” next to “rẽ”, since drivers here say quẹo trái / quẹo phải.

steps.why: The questions every new person will ask you. Answer them about your real life.

items: Anh ở Việt Nam bao lâu rồi?
How long have you been in Vietnam?
Tôi nói tiếng Việt một chút.

steps.teach: Your teacher interviews you for two minutes. Answer about your real life, even if it is slow.
steps.tg: Two-minute interview with the learner’s real details. Help them build their own answers (their district, their job) and save them in the app under “My answers”. Do not accept the book answers.

steps.vi: Truyện đầu tiên và mốc bắt đầu
steps.en: Your first story and your starting line
steps.why: You can now read a short story and record where you are. After this the full app opens.
steps.teach: Read the first chapter aloud to your teacher. Then listen together to your two-minute speaking sample and agree on the one thing to fix next.
steps.tg: Listen to the learner read chapter one aloud, then to their two-minute sample (on your teacher page). Agree on one priority for the next month and write it as a note to them. From here they use the full app with daily lengths of 30 to 90 minutes.

how: Vietnamese uses the alphabet you already know. What is new is the marks on the letters. Once you can read the marks, you can read anything out loud, even words you have never seen.
The tone is part of the word. Change the tone and it is a different word. These six are six different words:
Some marks change the vowel itself: ă â ê ô ơ ư. Others show the tone: á à ả ã ạ. One letter can carry both, like ấ or ở. You will learn the vowel marks in steps 3 and 4.
The app teaches southern Vietnamese, the way people in Saigon talk. Two things you will notice: the tones hỏi (ả) and ngã (ã) sound the same here, and d and gi sound like an English y.
Listen first. Say everything out loud, every time. Go slowly. Your teacher checks your sounds, and each step tells you what to do with them in class.
tones: Flat and fairly high. No mark.
Starts mid and rises. Like asking “yes?”.
Low and falling, relaxed. Like a tired “oh”.
Dips down, then comes back up.
ngã · in Saigon, the same as hỏi
In the south it sounds like hỏi. You still have to spell it right.
you: Neutral and polite. Always safe for a beginner.
you, to a man a bit older than you
Also what a man calls himself when talking to someone younger.
you, to a woman a bit older than you
Also what she calls herself to someone younger.
Also what you call yourself to anh or chị.
you, to a friend your own age
you, to a woman your parents’ age
you, to a man your parents’ age
A little younger than your father.
num: One to ten are single words. Learn them cold: một, hai, ba, bốn, năm, sáu, bảy, tám, chín, mười.
Twenty is hai mươi, thirty is ba mươi. In Saigon people usually say chục: hai chục, ba chục.
Prices are in thousands: ngàn. Năm chục ngàn is 50,000. Sellers often drop the word ngàn and just say “năm chục”.
